Example ID: 7482275
QUESTION:
Necrotizing fasciitis: an indication for hyperbaric oxygenation therapy?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] The accepted treatment protocol for necrotizing fasciitis (NF) consists of extensive surgery and wide spectrum antibiotics.
[1] Hyperbaric oxygenation (HBO) has been recommended as adjuvant therapy for NF, improving patient mortality and outcome.
[2] However, the beneficial effect of HBO for NF remains controversial.
[3] A retrospective evaluation of treatment outcome in 37 patients treated for NF between 1984 and 1993 was carried out.
[4] The mortality rate, morbidity criteria, and risk factors for grave prognosis were compared between a group of 25 patients who received HBO as part of their treatment protocol and a group of the remaining 12 patients treated by surgical excision and antibiotics alone.
[5] The two groups were found to be similar with regard to age, gender, the incidence of individual risk factors for ominous prognosis, and the Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II score for disease's severity on presentation.
[6] The mortality rate among the HBO-treated patients was 36%, as opposed to 25% in the non-HBO group.
[7] The mean number of surgical débridements required per patient was significantly higher in the HBO group: 3.3 compared with 1.5 in the non-HBO-treated patients.
[8] Although the average length of hospitalization for survivors was shorter for the HBO group, the difference between the groups did not reach statistical significance.

[8] Using ROC curves, we found that the 30-day data discriminated the top and bottom fifths of the 180-day data extremely well, especially for AMI outcomes.

[7] More preventive and therapeutic services were offered or performed at our residency training sites but fewer diagnostic services were performed.
[8] There were fewer consultations requested at our residency training sites but similar hospitalization rates for patients.
[9] The mean duration of visit differed by only 1 minute.

Example ID: 8262881
QUESTION:
Body dysmorphic disorder: does it have a psychotic subtype?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Although body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is classified in DSM-III-R as a nonpsychotic somatoform disorder, controversy exists as to whether BDD can present with psychotic features.
[1] If it can, this raises the possibility that its DSM-III-R psychotic counterpart-delusional disorder, somatic type--may not be a separate disorder.
[2] The purpose of this study was to determine whether patients with nonpsychotic BDD (defined according to DSM-III-R criteria, i.e., with maintenance of some insight) were different from patients with psychotic BDD (those whose preoccupation was without insight and of delusional intensity).
[3] Fifty consecutive patients meeting DSM-III-R criteria A and C for BDD were assessed with a semistructured interview and the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (SCID).
[4] Family histories of psychiatric disorders were blindly assessed.
[5] The 24 patients with nonpsychotic BDD were compared with the 26 patients with psychotic BDD with respect to demographics, phenomenology, course of illness, associated features, comorbid psychiatric disorders, family history, and treatment response.
[6] Patients with psychotic BDD displayed a significantly higher rate of lifetime DSM-III-R psychotic disorder diagnoses than patients with nonpsychotic BDD.
[7] However, the two groups did not differ significantly on most other variables examined.
[8] For instance, both psychotic and nonpsychotic patients displayed significant morbidity;
[9] high comorbidity with mood, anxiety, and psychoactive substance use disorders;
[10] and apparent preferential response to serotonin reuptake inhibitors rather than to non-serotonin reuptake blocking antidepressants or antipsychotics.

[4] There were no significant differences in the incidence of intrahepatic metastasis, or portal vein invasion.

[6] The transparent specimen showed that the portal vein in the tumor seemed to be intact.
[7] Microscopically, cancer cell infiltration into the fibrous frame of the portal tract was present.
[8] There were no significant differences in the disease free survival between the two groups.
[9] An analysis of tumor volume doubling time in recurrent foci suggested that minute cancerous foci had been present at the time of operation.

Are endothelial cell patterns of astrocytomas indicative of grade?

[4] All tumor cases showed cells positive for GFAP.

[0] To investigate whether the presence of hippocampal atrophy (HCA) on MRI in Alzheimer's disease (AD) leads to a more rapid decline in cognitive function.

[2] A prospective follow-up of subjects from a previously reported MRI study.

[4] They were followed up at approximately 2 years with repeat cognitive testing, blind to initial diagnosis and MRI result.
[5] HCA was rated by two radiologists blind to cognitive test score results.
[6] Cognitive assessment was by the Cambridge Cognitive Examination (CAMCOG).
[7] No significant differences in rate of cognitive decline, mortality or progression to dementia were found between subjects with or without HCA.

[0] Uterus-specific synthetic Prostaglandin analogues (gemeprost, sulproston etc.) have been widely employed for termination of pregnancy in the second trimester.

[8] The requirement of Pethidin and the intensity of pain (measured by pain scale according to Huskisson) especially in the late first stage of labour were not statistically different between both groups.
[9] Side effects of paracervical anaesthesia did not occur.

[4] We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of LUS in comparison with preoperative staging and laparoscopy in 33 patients with colorectal cancer.
[5] Preoperative staging included abdominal US, CT, and endoscopic US (for rectal cancer).
[6] Laparoscopy and LUS were performed in all cases.
[7] Pre- and intraoperative staging were related to definitive histology.
[8] Staging was done according to the TNM classification.
[9] LUS obtained good results in the evaluation of hepatic metastases, with a sensitivity of 100% versus 62.5% and 75% by preoperative diagnostic means and laparoscopy, respectively.
[10] Nodal metastases were diagnosed with a sensitivity of 94% versus 18% with preoperative staging and 6% with laparoscopy, but the method had a low specificity (53%).
[11] The therapeutic program was changed thanks to laparoscopy and LUS in 11 cases (33%).
[12] In four cases (12%), the planned therapeutic approach was changed after LUS alone.

[5] The results are based on observations of 4793 men and 4313 women.

[9] The study of adjusted risk ratios for four groups of subjects defined on the basis of their baseline serum chloride levels revealed a decreasing log-linear 'dose-response' relation to total and cardiovascular mortalities.

Example ID: 11413427
QUESTION:
Does transverse apex coincide with coronal apex levels (regional or global) in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] To identify the regional and global apexes of curves in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis and to compare the levels of those with the most rotated vertebral levels on computed tomography scans.
[1] The terminology regarding the terms and definitions had been arbitrary until being refined and standardized by the Scoliosis Research Society Working Group on Three-Dimensional Terminology of Spinal Deformity.
[2] Apical vertebra or disc is defined as the most laterally deviated vertebra or disc in a scoliosis curve, but the most rotated vertebra (or disc) has not been included in this terminology.
[3] One study suggested that the most rotated vertebral level was always located at the apex.
[4] Thirty-three structural curves of 25 consecutive patients scheduled for surgery for thoracic or thoracolumbar scoliosis were analyzed with standing anteroposterior radiographs and computed tomography scans covering the curve apexes and pelvis.
[5] Thoracic and lumbar curves were evaluated separately for all Type II curves.
[6] Vertebral rotations were normalized by the rotation of the pelvis.
[7] The most rotated vertebral (or disc) levels (transverse apex) were compared with the regional and global apex levels (vertebra or disc) (coronal apexes) of the corresponding curves separately.

[2] Interleukin-8 is elevated in the lung within 2 hrs of major trauma in patients who later develop ARDS, and thus it plays a central role in the recruitment of neutrophils to the lung and their subsequent activation.
[3] We hypothesized that enhanced interleukin-8-mediated neutrophil migratory activity in the early postinjury phase, before the development of ARDS, may be a crucial factor in the etiology of ARDS.
[4] Prospective observational study.

[7] Adult blunt trauma victims with Injury Severity Score>or = 18.

[9] Identical samples were obtained from normal laboratory volunteers (n = 9).
[10] The neutrophil count in each specimen was measured, and the number of neutrophils migrating across porous tissue culture inserts in response to defined concentrations of interleukin-8 (0, 10, 30, and 100 ng/mL) was quantitated by peroxidase assay.
[11] Neutrophil counts in the whole blood specimens obtained from those later developing ARDS were elevated significantly at admission and declined rapidly throughout the next 24 hrs.
[12] Significantly greater numbers of trauma patients' neutrophils migrated to concentrations of interleukin-8 (30 and 100 ng/mL) at each time point when compared with normal volunteers (Mann-Whitney U test, p<.05).
[13] Neutrophils isolated from major trauma patients exhibited an enhanced migratory response to high concentrations of interleukin-8 throughout the first 24 hrs of admission, in contrast to the normal physiologic attenuation of migration seen in neutrophils isolated from normal laboratory volunteers.

QUESTION:
Is withdrawal-induced anxiety in alcoholism based on beta-endorphin deficiency?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Associations between several psychopathological alterations and lowered beta-endorphin(beta E) plasma levels have already been stated in former studies.
[1] However, whereas single measures during static conditions generally failed in linking beta E levels with psychopathology, dynamic changes of beta E in particular have been shown to be associated with spells of anxiety and depression.
[2] During alcohol withdrawal, a decreased secretion of beta E with a delayed normalization has been reported, but up to now only few data became available regarding the interaction of plasma beta E and psychopathological parameters.
[3] The aim of our study was to test the hypothesis whether beta E during acute alcohol withdrawal is associated with anxiety, depression, and craving.
[4] We observed self-rated anxiety, depression, and craving during alcohol withdrawal and assessed beta E levels (RIA) in a consecutive sample of 60 alcoholics on day 1 and day 14 after onset of withdrawal, and in 30 healthy volunteers.
[5] To control for mutual interactions of beta E and the pituitary-adrenocortical hormone secretion, plasma corticotropin (ACTH) and cortisol were also determined.
[6] In accordance with prior studies, beta E was significantly lowered on day 1 and day 14 of alcohol withdrawal relative to controls.
[7] Plasma levels of ACTH correlated significantly with beta E in alcoholics at both time points and in controls, without differing significantly between the groups.
[8] Self-rated anxiety, depression, and alcohol craving decreased significantly between day 1 and day 14.
[9] Levels of beta E were inversely correlated with anxiety day 1 (r=-0.58) and day 14 (r=-0.71).
[10] Partial correlation coefficients controlling for ACTH plasma levels revealed that this correlation was largely independent from ACTH.
[11] In addition, a significant inverse relationship was found between beta E and craving on day 14 (r=-0.28).
[12] No association appeared between beta E and depression.

[4] When tumor size is dichotomized, this effect should be most pronounced in the large size (>5 cm) group in which the size span is larger.
[5] We analyzed the associations between tumor size and depth and the prognostic importance of grade, size and depth in a population-based series of 490 adult patients with soft tissue sarcoma of the extremity or trunk wall with complete, 4.5 years minimum, follow-up.

[7] The mean size of small tumors was the same whether superficial or deep but the mean size of large and deep-seated tumors were one third larger than that of large but superficial tumors.
[8] Tumor depth influenced the prognosis in the subset of high-grade and large tumors.
[9] In this subset deep-seated tumors had poorer survival rate than superficial tumors, which could be explained by the larger mean size of the deep-seated tumors.

[8] Tumor depth influenced the prognosis in the subset of high-grade and large tumors.
[9] In this subset deep-seated tumors had poorer survival rate than superficial tumors, which could be explained by the larger mean size of the deep-seated tumors.

Quality of life in lung cancer patients: does socioeconomic status matter?

[0] As part of a prospective study on quality of life in newly diagnosed lung cancer patients an investigation was carried out to examine whether there were differences among patients' quality of life scores and their socioeconomic status.

[4] In all, 129 lung cancer patients entered into the study.
[5] Of these data for 82 patients were complete (at baseline and follow-up).
[6] 57% of patients were of lower socioeconomic status and they had more health problems, less functioning, and more symptoms as compared to affluent patients.
[7] Of these, physical mobility (P = 0.05), energy (P = 0.01), role functioning (P = 0.04), physical functioning (P = 0.03), and breathlessness (P = 0.02) were significant at baseline.
[8] However, at follow-up assessment there was no significant difference between patient groups nor did any consistent pattern emerge.

[8] For poorly differentiated disease, potentially curative therapy resulted in LE and QALE gains up to age 80 years.

[10] When cohort and pooled case series data were used, RP was preferred over EBRT in all groups but was comparable to modern radiotherapy.

[7] The blood pressures and HR were measured simultaneously.
[8] For the analysis, HR, PWV, compliance (C), and compliance index (Ci) were converted as percent changes (delta) from the baseline values.
[9] Percent changes of the parameters of the aortic stiffness, i.e., deltaPWV, deltaC, and deltaCi, were grouped by every 10% increase in deltaHR.
[10] There was no significant difference among groups in deltaPWV, deltaC and deltaCi (p>0.05 for each of the group).
[11] The regression analysis showed no significant correlation of deltaHR with deltaPWV and deltaC (r = 0.18, 0.13 respectively, p>0.05 for each).
[12] deltaCi had a poor correlation with deltaHR (r = 0.22, p<0.05).
[13] However, only 4.6% of deltaCi could be referred to deltaHR (r2 = 0.046).

[8] Treatment of uveal melanoma cell lines with STI571, which blocks c-kit autophosphorylation, resulted in cell death.
[9] The IC(50) of the inhibitory effects on c-kit phosphorylation and cell proliferation was of equal size and less than 2.5 microM.

[10] There was a clear relationship between the changes in spasticity and in arm function in patients treated with botulinum toxin (Dysport) at 500 or 1000 units (rho = -0.5679, p = 0.0090, n = 22;
[11] rho = -0.4430, p = 0.0018, n = 47), but not in those treated with placebo or 1500 units.

[10] Femoral rollback was not significantly affected by either unicompartmental or tricompartmental arthroplasty.
[11] Quadriceps tension was also similar among all three conditions.

[10] The highest level of IL-15 expression was also seen in biopsies taken during bleeding.
[11] No clear relationship between killer Ig like receptor genotype and bleeding on HT was observed.

[9] At rest, no significant group differences were seen.

[8] Microsatellite instability and MLH1 promoter methylation analyses were performed on a subset of cases.
[9] Two patients met Amsterdam criteria for HNPCC.
[10] Five additional patients, all medium-risk, had molecular findings consistent with a germline mutation of either MSH2 or MLH1.
[11] None of the low-risk patients had molecular results consistent with a germline mutation.

[10] The area under the receiver operator curve was 72.4%, showing that the model was adequate.

[3] Abridged lifetables for the period 1999-2003 were constructed using standard demographic methods for each of four ethnic groups (Asian, Pacific, Maori and European) by NZDep2001 quintile and sex.
[4] Gradients were estimated by fitting generalised linear models to the quintile-specific life expectancy estimates for each ethnic group (by sex).
[5] The contribution of variation in deprivation distributions to inter-ethnic inequalities in life expectancy was estimated by re-weighting the quintile-specific mortality rates for each ethnic group using weights derived from the European deprivation distribution and recalculating the lifetable.
[6] All four ethnic groups exhibit deprivation gradients in all-cause mortality (life expectancy).
[7] Maori show the steepest gradients, with slopes approximately 25% steeper than those of Europeans for both males and females.
[8] By contrast, gradients among Asian and Pacific peoples are shallower than those of their European counterparts.

Is fluoroscopy essential for retrieval of lower ureteric stones?

[0] The aim of this study was to assess the efficacy of ureteroscopy for lower ureteric stones without the use of fluoroscopy.

[3] Whenever required, the ureteric meatus was dilated with a ureteric balloon under direct vision.
[4] Double-J stent placement was done with the aid of ureteroscopy.
[5] A fluoroscope was kept standby.
[6] The patients had a postoperative X-ray of the kidney-ureter-bladder region to document the stone clearance.
[7] The mean stone size was 8.7 mm (range 6-15).
[8] Complete clearance without the use of fluoroscopy was achieved in 99 patients (94.2%).
[9] Fluoroscopy was required in 6 patients (4%) for calcified stricture (n = 1), duplex system (n = 1), narrow and tortuous meatus causing difficulty in passing the 5-Fr balloon dilator (n = 3), and confirmation of spontaneous passage of the stone (n = 1).
[10] Of the 13 patients who required balloon dilatation it was successfully achieved without fluoroscopy.
[11] Double-J stenting was done due to mucosal ulceration (n = 3), polypoid reaction (n = 2), and perforation (n = 1).
[12] All these patients had correct placement of the stent, as confirmed by X-ray of the kidney-ureter-bladder region postoperatively.

[2] Group 1 (recurrent spontaneous abortion) consisted of 357 women with 2 or more spontaneous losses.
[3] In group 2 (infertility), there were 349 subjects from infertility practices recruited at the time of a positive serum beta-human chorionic gonadotropin.
[4] Group 3 (spontaneous abortion) women (n = 81) were recruited at the time of an ultrasound diagnosis of an embryonic demise or an anembryonic gestation.
[5] Groups 4 (primiparous) and 5 (multiparous) were healthy pregnant subjects previously enrolled in another study to determine the incidence and cause of pregnancy complications, such as preeclampsia and intrauterine growth restriction.
[6] The Primiparous group included 114 women in their first pregnancy, whereas the Multiparous group consisted of 79 women with 2 or more pregnancies but without pregnancy loss.
[7] The rate of extreme skewing (90% or greater) in the recurrent spontaneous abortion population was 8.6%, and not statistically different from any of the other groups, except the Primiparous group (1.0%, P<.01).
[8] The incidence of X-inactivation skewing of 90% or greater was no different whether there had been at least 1 live birth (9.9%), or no previous live births and at least 3 losses (5.6%, P>.05).
[9] When age and skewing of 90% or greater are compared, subjects with extreme skewing have a mean age of 2 years older than those without extreme skewing (P<.05).

[13] 95% confidence interval, 2.13 to 13.42).

Example ID: 18086459
QUESTION:
Long-term significance of postictal psychotic episodes II. Are they predictive of interictal psychotic episodes?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] The aim of this study was to determine whether postictal psychotic episodes (PIPE) are predictive of the development of interictal psychotic episodes (IPE).
[1] This was a retrospective study of 18 consecutive adults with a partial seizure disorder and PIPE (study group) and 36 patients with a partial seizure disorder but without PIPE (control group).
[2] These two groups were compared with respect to the likelihood of developing IPE over an 8-year follow-up period and the variables operant in the development of IPE.
[3] Statistical analyses consisted of logistic regression models to identify the variables predictive of the development of IPE.
[4] Predictors included: number and location of ictal foci, seizure type, etiology, age at seizure onset, duration of seizure disorder, MRI abnormalities, and psychiatric history prior to the index video/EEG monitoring (other than PIPE).
[5] Seven patients with PIPE and one control patient went on to develop an IPE.
[6] Predictors of IPE in univariate logistic regression analyses included a history of PIPE (P=0.006), male gender (P=0.028), and having bilateral ictal foci (P=0.048).
[7] Significance disappeared for all of these variables when they were entered into a multivariate analysis.

[6] Despite reducing some of the risk for corneal haze compared to conventional PRK, ASA cases still can develop corneal haze or breakthrough haze from the hypercellular fibrotic stromal scarring.
[7] In contrast, similar to conventional LASIK, SBK still has the short- and long-term potential for interface wound complications from the hypocellular primitive stromal scar.

[9] Lactate was higher for RRP at T2 (P = 0.001), T3 (P = 0.001) and T4 (P = 0.004), although remaining within the normal ranges.
[10] IL-1 alpha did not change at the different sample times.

[11] Gender remained an independent risk factor in young and old subgroup analysis, with the protection afforded by female gender remaining unchanged.

Can calprotectin predict relapse risk in inflammatory bowel disease?

[0] Assessing the clinical course of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients consists of periodical clinical evaluations and laboratory tests.

[4] The cutoff level was set at 130 mg/kg of feces.
[5] Patients were followed up for 1 yr after the test or until relapse.
[6] The cumulative proportion of relapses was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier analysis.
[7] Statistics for equality of survival distribution were tested using the log-rank test.
[8] The calprotectin test was positive in 44 UC patients and 26 of them relapsed within a year, while 11 of 53 UC patients with a negative calprotectin test relapsed within the same time frame.

[10] A significant correlation emerged between a positive calprotectin test and the probability of relapse in UC patients (P= 0.000).
[11] In CD patients, only cases of colonic CD showed a significant correlation between a positive calprotectin test and the probability of relapse, i.e., 6 colonic CD patients were positive for the calprotectin test and 4 relapsed (P= 0.02).

Does ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament affect the neurological outcome after traumatic cervical cord injury?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Retrospective outcome measurement study.
[1] The purpose of this study is to assess whether ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL) affects neurologic outcomes in patients with acute cervical spinal cord injury (SCI).
[2] There have so far been few reports examining the relationship between OPLL and SCI and there is controversy regarding the deteriorating effects of OPLL-induced canal stenosis on neurologic outcomes.
[3] To obtain a relatively uniform background, patients nonsurgically treated for an acute C3-C4 level SCI without any fractures or dislocations of the spinal column were selected, resulting in 129 patients.
[4] There were 110 men and 19 women (mean age was 61.1 years), having various neurologic conditions on admission (American Spinal Injury Association [ASIA] impairment scale A, 43;
[5] The follow-up period was the duration of their hospital stay and ranged from 50 to 603 days (mean, 233 days).
[6] The presence of OPLL, the cause of injury, the degree of canal stenosis (both static and dynamic), and the neurologic outcomes in motor function, including improvement rate, were assessed.
[7] Of the 129 patients investigated in this study, OPLL was identified at the site of the injury in 13 patients (10.1%).
[8] In this OPLL+ group, the static and dynamic canal diameters at C3 and C4 were significantly smaller than those of the remaining 116 patients (OPLL- group).
[9] However, no significant difference was observed between the 2 groups in terms of ASIA motor score both at the time of administration and discharge, and the mean improvement rate in ASIA motor score was 55.5 +/- 9.0% in OPLL+ group, while it was 43.1 +/- 2.8% in the OPLL-group.
[10] Furthermore, no significant correlation was observed between the static/dynamic canal diameters and neurologic outcome in all 129 patients.

[3] This was a cross-sectional study in which 96 men aged 40 or more of the South Metropolitan Region of Santiago de Chile were surveyed with the Androgen Deficiency of Aging Men (ADAM) questionnaire of the Saint Louis University and sampled for the serum determination of total testosterone, sexual hormone binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin.
[4] Also free and bioavailable testosterone were calculated.

[7] A total of 78 men (81.3%) were identified as possible PADAM according to the ADAM questionnaire.
[8] Total testosterone levels fell from 503.6+/-180.1 ng/dL in men aged 40 to 54 years to 382.1+/-247.3 in those>70 years;
[9] however this was not statistically significant (ANOVA, p=0.06).

[11] Overall (n=96), available testosterone confirmed PADAM diagnosis in 27 cases (28.1%).
[12] The ADAM tool rendered a 83.3% sensitivity and 19.7% specificity in the detection of PADAM.
[13] Item 1 (decreased sexual desire) was a better predictor of hypogonadism than the complete questionnaire (63.3% sensitivity and 66.7% specificity).

Example ID: 19757704
QUESTION:
Is Chaalia/Pan Masala harmful for health?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] To determine the practices and knowledge of harmful effects regarding use of Chaalia and Pan Masala in three schools of Mahmoodabad and Chanesar Goth, Jamshed Town, Karachi, Pakistan.
[1] To achieve the objective a cross-sectional design was used in three government schools of Mahmoodabad and Chanesar Goth, Jamshed Town, Karachi.
[2] Students of either gender drawn from these schools fulfilling the inclusion and exclusion criteria were interviewed using a pre-coded structured questionnaire.
[3] Along with demographic data, questions regarding frequency of Chaalia and Pan Masala use, practices of this habit in friends and family and place of procurement of these substances, were inquired.
[4] Knowledge was assessed about harmful effects and its source of information.
[5] In addition, practices in relation to that knowledge were assessed.
[6] A total of 370 students were interviewed over a period of six weeks, of which 205 (55.4%) were boys.
[7] The ages of the students were between 10 and 15 years.
[8] Thirty one percent of the fathers and 62% of the mothers were uneducated.
[9] The frequency of use of any brand of Chaalia was found to be 94% and that of Pan Masala was 73.8%.
[10] Eighty five percent of them were regular users.
[11] A large majority (88%) procured the substances themselves from near their homes.
[12] Ninety five percent of the children had friends with the same habits.
[13] Eighty four percent were using the substances in full knowledge of their families.
[14] Chaalia was considered harmful for health by 96% and Pan Masala by 60%.
[15] Good taste was cited as a reason for continuing the habit by 88.5% of the children and use by friends by 57%.

[0] Obesity may be associated with lower prostate specific antigen through hemodilution.
[1] We examined the relationship between body mass index and prostate specific antigen by age in men without prostate cancer in a longitudinal aging study to determine whether prostate specific antigen must be adjusted for body mass index.
[2] The study population included 994 men (4,937 observations) without prostate cancer in the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging.
[3] Mixed effects models were used to examine the relationship between prostate specific antigen and body mass index in kg/m(2) by age.
[4] Separate models were explored in men with prostate cancer censored at diagnosis, for percent body fat measurements, for weight changes with time and adjusting for initial prostate size in 483 men (2,523 observations) with pelvic magnetic resonance imaging measurements.
[5] In men without prostate cancer body mass index was not significantly associated with prostate specific antigen after adjusting for age (p = 0.06).
[6] A 10-point body mass index increase was associated with a prostate specific antigen difference of -0.03 ng/ml (95% CI -0.40-0.49).
[7] Results were similar when men with prostate cancer were included, when percent body fat was substituted for body mass index, and after adjusting for prostate volume.
[8] Longitudinal weight changes also had no significant association with prostate specific antigen.

[0] Peripheral venous thrombophlebitis (PVT) is a common complication of intravenous cannulation, occurring in about 30% of patients.

[3] Informed consent was obtained from all of them.
[4] Cannulae in the control group were removed only if the site became painful, the cannula got dislodged or there were signs and symptoms suggestive of PVT, namely pain, erythema, swelling, excessive warmth or a palpable venous cord.

[6] All the patients were examined every 24 hours for signs and symptoms of PVT at the current and previous sites of infusion.
[7] The incidence of PVT was 100% (21/21) in the control group and only 9.5% (2/21) in the study group (p<0.0001).

Example ID: 20101129
QUESTION:
Is prophylactic fixation a cost-effective method to prevent a future contralateral fragility hip fracture?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] : A previous hip fracture more than doubles the risk of a contralateral hip fracture.
[1] Pharmacologic and environmental interventions to prevent hip fracture have documented poor compliance.
[2] The purpose of this study was to examine the cost-effectiveness of prophylactic fixation of the uninjured hip to prevent contralateral hip fracture.
[3] : A Markov state-transition model was used to evaluate the cost and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) for unilateral fixation of hip fracture alone (including internal fixation or arthroplasty) compared with unilateral fixation and contralateral prophylactic hip fixation performed at the time of hip fracture or unilateral fixation and bilateral hip pad protection.
[4] Prophylactic fixation involved placement of a cephalomedullary nail in the uninjured hip and was initially assumed to have a relative risk of a contralateral fracture of 1%.
[5] Health states included good health, surgery-related complications requiring a second operation (infection, osteonecrosis, nonunion, and malunion), fracture of the uninjured hip, and death.
[6] The primary outcome measure was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio estimated as cost per QALY gained in 2006 US dollars with incremental cost-effectiveness ratios below $50,000 per QALY gained considered cost-effective.
[7] Sensitivity analyses evaluated the impact of patient age, annual mortality and complication rates, intervention effectiveness, utilities, and costs on the value of prophylactic fixation.
[8] : In the baseline analysis, in a 79-year-old woman, prophylactic fixation was not found to be cost-effective (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio = $142,795/QALY).
[9] However, prophylactic fixation was found to be a cost-effective method to prevent contralateral hip fracture in: 1) women 71 to 75 years old who had 30% greater relative risk for a contralateral fracture;
[10] and 2) women younger than age 70 years.
[11] Cost-effectiveness was greater when the additional costs of prophylaxis were less than $6000.
[12] However, for most analyses, the success of prophylactic fixation was highly sensitive to the effectiveness and the relative morbidity and mortality of the additional procedure.

[8] After adjusting for age, institution, postgraduate year, and knowledge of parental leave policies, women were less likely to plan to have children during residency (odds ratio 0.46 [95% confidence interval 0.25-0.84]).
[9] In mediation analysis, threats to career explained 67% of the gender variance.

Should temperature be monitorized during kidney allograft preservation?

[0] It is generally considered that kidney grafts should be preserved at 4 degrees C during cold storage.

[3] Temperature was monitored using the Thermobouton probe during preservation of pig kidneys, in the same conditions used with human grafts.
[4] The probe recorded the temperature level every 10 minutes during four days.
[5] We compared the results found with the new storage can with results obtained in the same conditions with the storage can formerly used by our team.
[6] We also studied the best position of the probe for temperature monitoring and the influence of the amount of ice within the transport pack on the temperature level.
[7] We then monitored the temperature during the conservation of actual human kidney grafts harvested at our institution from August 2007 to May 2008.
[8] The temperature levels were the same regardless of the position of the probe within the transport pack.
[9] The lowest temperature was maintained during 15 hours, and the temperature level stayed below 5 degrees C for 57 hours with the new storage can.
[10] The former storage can maintained the lowest temperature level for 80 minutes, and temperature reached 5 degrees C after 10 hours 40 minutes.
[11] Temperature levels were similar when 2 or 4 kg of crushed ice were used.
[12] We observed similar results when monitoring the conservation of human grafts.

[14] Finally, leptin-induced NADPH oxidase activation promoted macrophage proliferation.

[0] Tethering of the spinal cord is thought to increase the chance of neurological injury when scoliosis correction is undertaken.

[5] The minimum follow-up after fusion was 2 years.
[6] Charts and radiographs were reviewed for neurological or shunt complications in the perioperative period.
[7] The average age of the patients was 12.4 years, and the following neurological levels were affected: T-12 and above, 7 patients;
[8] All were radiographically tethered as confirmed on MR imaging.
[9] Fourteen of the patients (82%) had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt.
[10] The mean Cobb angle was corrected from 82 degrees to 35 degrees , for a 57% correction.
[11] All patients underwent neuromonitoring of their upper extremities, and some underwent lower extremity monitoring as well.
[12] Postoperatively, no patient experienced a new cranial nerve palsy, shunt malfunction, change in urological function, or upper extremity weakness/sensory loss.
[13] One patient had transient lower extremity weakness, which returned to baseline within 1 month of surgery.

[8] Study 2: P = .001, standardized effect size = 0.31;
[9] Study 3: P = .009, standardized effect size = 0.13.
[10] In Study 2, perspective-taking improved African American SPs' satisfaction.
[11] In Study 3, intervention students with high baseline perspective-taking tendencies outscored controls (P = .0004, standardized effect size = 0.25), whereas those with low perspective-taking tendencies did not (P = .72, standardized effect size = 0.00).

[12] Fondaparinux may have a role in bridge therapy for these patients.

[7] Patients with a normal hematocrit had a reduced hospital LOS, compared with those with severe, moderate, and mild anemia (p<0.01).
[8] A history of cardiovascular disease did not significantly influence these findings.

[11] PCNA expression was seen in 65% of GBC cases and 11% of XGC, but not in chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladders.

[13] Beta-catenin expression was positive in the GBC, XGC, chronic cholecystitis and control gallbladder groups.

Do mitochondria play a role in remodelling lace plant leaves during programmed cell death?

[3] PCD occurs in the cells at the center of these areoles and progresses outwards, stopping approximately five cells from the vasculature.
[4] The role of mitochondria during PCD has been recognized in animals;
[5] however, it has been less studied during PCD in plants.
[6] The following paper elucidates the role of mitochondrial dynamics during developmentally regulated PCD in vivo in A.
[7] A single areole within a window stage leaf (PCD is occurring) was divided into three areas based on the progression of PCD;
[8] cells that will not undergo PCD (NPCD), cells in early stages of PCD (EPCD), and cells in late stages of PCD (LPCD).
[9] Window stage leaves were stained with the mitochondrial dye MitoTracker Red CMXRos and examined.
[10] Mitochondrial dynamics were delineated into four categories (M1-M4) based on characteristics including distribution, motility, and membrane potential (ΔΨm).
[11] A TUNEL assay showed fragmented nDNA in a gradient over these mitochondrial stages.
[12] Chloroplasts and transvacuolar strands were also examined using live cell imaging.
[13] The possible importance of mitochondrial permeability transition pore (PTP) formation during PCD was indirectly examined via in vivo cyclosporine A (CsA) treatment.
[14] This treatment resulted in lace plant leaves with a significantly lower number of perforations compared to controls, and that displayed mitochondrial dynamics similar to that of non-PCD cells.

[0] Ischemia-reperfusion (IR) injury remains a major cause of early morbidity and mortality after lung transplantation with poorly documented extrapulmonary repercussions.
[1] To determine the hemodynamic effect due to lung IR injury, we performed a quantitative coronary blood-flow analysis in a swine model of in situ lung ischemia and reperfusion.
[2] In 14 healthy pigs, blood flow was measured in the ascending aorta, left anterior descending (LAD), circumflex (Cx), right coronary artery (RCA), right common carotid artery (RCCA), and left internal mammary artery (LIMA), along with left-and right-ventricular pressures (LVP and RVP), aortic pressure (AoP), and pulmonary artery pressure (PAP).
[3] Cardiac Troponin (cTn), interleukin 6 and 10 (IL-6 and IL-10), and tumor necrosis factor A (TNF-A) were measured in coronary sinus blood samples.
[4] The experimental (IR) group (n=10) underwent 60 min of lung ischemia followed by 60 min of reperfusion by clamping and releasing the left pulmonary hilum.
[5] Simultaneous measurements of all parameters were made at baseline and during IR.
[6] The control group (n=4) had similar measurements without lung IR.
[7] In the IR group, total coronary flow (TCF=LAD+Cx+RCA blood-flow) decreased precipitously and significantly from baseline (113±41 ml min"1) during IR (p<0.05), with the lowest value observed at 60 min of reperfusion (-37.1%, p<0.003).
[8] Baseline cTn (0.08±0.02 ng ml(-1)) increased during IR and peaked at 45 min of reperfusion (+138%, p<0.001).
[9] Baseline IL-6 (9.2±2.17 pg ml(-1)) increased during IR and peaked at 60 min of reperfusion (+228%, p<0.0001).
[10] Significant LVP drop at 5 min of ischemia (p<0.05) was followed by a slow return to baseline at 45 min of ischemia.
[11] A second LVP drop occurred at reperfusion (p<0.05) and persisted.
[12] Conversely, RVP increased throughout ischemia (p<0.05) and returned toward baseline during reperfusion.

[12] 38.8% of the restorative proctocolectomy group and 51.4% the ileorectal group had surgery for desmoid tumor complications (P = .21), and 22.4% and 22.2% of patients ultimately had permanent stomas.
[13] This study was limited by the relatively small numbers of patients.

Does a preoperative medically supervised weight loss program improve bariatric surgery outcomes?

[0] Many insurance payors mandate that bariatric surgery candidates undergo a medically supervised weight management (MSWM) program as a prerequisite for surgery.
[1] However, there is little evidence to support this requirement.

[3] This pilot randomized trial was conducted in a large academic urban public hospital.
[4] Patients who met NIH consensus criteria for bariatric surgery and whose insurance did not require a mandatory 6-month MSWM program were randomized to a MSWM program with monthly visits over 6 months (individual or group) or usual care for 6 months and then followed for bariatric surgery outcomes postoperatively.
[5] Demographics, weight, and patient behavior scores, including patient adherence, eating behavior, patient activation, and physical activity, were collected at baseline and at 6 months (immediately preoperatively and postoperatively).
[6] A total of 55 patients were enrolled in the study with complete follow-up on 23 patients.
[7] Participants randomized to a MSWM program attended an average of 2 sessions preoperatively.
[8] The majority of participants were female and non-Caucasian, mean age was 46 years, average income was less than $20,000/year, and most had Medicaid as their primary insurer, consistent with the demographics of the hospital's bariatric surgery program.
[9] Data analysis included both intention-to-treat and completers' analyses.
[10] No significant differences in weight loss and most patient behaviors were found between the two groups postoperatively, suggesting that participation in a MSWM program did not improve weight loss outcomes for LAGB.
[11] Participation in a MSWM program did appear to have a positive effect on physical activity postoperatively.

[0] The International Association of the Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups (IADPSG) recently recommended new criteria for diagnosing gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM).
[1] This study was undertaken to determine whether adopting the IADPSG criteria would be cost-effective, compared with the current standard of care.
[2] We developed a decision analysis model comparing the cost-utility of three strategies to identify GDM: 1) no screening, 2) current screening practice (1-h 50-g glucose challenge test between 24 and 28 weeks followed by 3-h 100-g glucose tolerance test when indicated), or 3) screening practice proposed by the IADPSG.
[3] Assumptions included that 1) women diagnosed with GDM received additional prenatal monitoring, mitigating the risks of preeclampsia, shoulder dystocia, and birth injury;
[4] and 2) GDM women had opportunity for intensive postdelivery counseling and behavior modification to reduce future diabetes risks.
[5] The primary outcome measure was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER).
[6] Our model demonstrates that the IADPSG recommendations are cost-effective only when postdelivery care reduces diabetes incidence.
[7] For every 100,000 women screened, 6,178 quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) are gained, at a cost of $125,633,826.
[8] The ICER for the IADPSG strategy compared with the current standard was $20,336 per QALY gained.

[10] In the matched-pair analysis of patients receiving LE, improvement of motor function occurred in 20% after LE + RT and 23% after RT alone (p = 0.06).
[11] The 1-year local control rates were 50% and 92% (p = 0.33).
[12] The 1-year survival rates were 32% and 32% (p = 0.55).

Example ID: 22453060
QUESTION:
Does a 4 diagram manual enable laypersons to operate the Laryngeal Mask Supreme®?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Bystander resuscitation plays an important role in lifesaving cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).
[1] A significant reduction in the "no-flow-time", quantitatively better chest compressions and an improved quality of ventilation can be demonstrated during CPR using supraglottic airway devices (SADs).
[2] Previous studies have demonstrated the ability of inexperienced persons to operate SADs after brief instruction.
[3] The aim of this pilot study was to determine whether an instruction manual consisting of four diagrams enables laypersons to operate a Laryngeal Mask Supreme® (LMAS) in the manikin.
[4] An instruction manual of four illustrations with speech bubbles displaying the correct use of the LMAS was designed.
[5] Laypersons were handed a bag containing a LMAS, a bag mask valve device (BMV), a syringe prefilled with air and the instruction sheet, and were asked to perform and ventilate the manikin as displayed.
[6] Time to ventilation was recorded and degree of success evaluated.
[7] A total of 150 laypersons took part.
[8] Overall 145 participants (96.7%) inserted the LMAS in the manikin in the right direction.
[9] The device was inserted inverted or twisted in 13 (8.7%) attempts.
[10] Eight (5.3%) individuals recognized this and corrected the position.
[11] Within the first 2 minutes 119 (79.3%) applicants were able to insert the LMAS and provide tidal volumes greater than 150 ml (estimated dead space).
[12] Time to insertion and first ventilation was 83.2 ± 29 s.
[13] No significant difference related to previous BLS training (P = 0.85), technical education (P = 0.07) or gender could be demonstrated (P = 0.25).

[9] Waist circumference was another predictor of BP changes [β = 0.18 cm (95% CI: 0.05-0.24)]and CSWA.
[10] HIV infection was inversely associated with increased BP.

[9] In contrast, there was no difference in 25(OH)D level between non-obese CD patients and non-obese normal children (28.39 +/- 10.26 versus 30.64 +/-12.08, p = 0.52).
[10] The season of 25(OH)D measurement was not a significant confounder (p =0.7).

[9] A scoring system was developed using these features to stratify the severity of the injury.
[10] Patients with isolated extension deformity, but none of the other features, were more likely to complete successful nonoperative management.

[11] RHR was significantly associated with age, waist circumference, and BP.
[12] Individuals with an elevated RHR had a higher risk (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.15-3.26%, p = 0.013) of casual high BP compared with participants with normal RHR independently of several established CVD risk factors.
[13] The regression dilution ratio of RHR was 0.75 (95% CI 0.62-0.89).

Example ID: 23149821

Should HIV-infected patients be screened for silent myocardial ischaemia using gated myocardial perfusion SPECT?

[2] The prevalence of SMI detected by myocardial SPECT was determined in 94 HIV-infected patients with a normal clinical cardiovascular examination in relation to anthropomorphic parameters, CRFs, inflammatory and HIV infection status, and treatment.
[3] Coronary artery disease was detected in nine patients (eight with ischaemia, one with myocardial infarction), corresponding to 9.6 % positivity.
[4] All but two of the scintigraphic diagnoses of ischaemia were confirmed by coronarography.

[6] According to multivariate analysis, the only independent parameter significantly associated with the scintigraphic diagnosis of SMI was the combination of gender and age (p = 0.01).
[7] All the positive myocardial SPECT scans were in men older than 52 years with at least two other CRFs.
[8] In this subpopulation of 47 patients, the prevalence of SMI detected by myocardial SPECT reached 19.2 %.

[7] Lack of consistent and standardized assessment data, insufficiency analysis that carried out showed improved functional outcomes (P < 0.05) in operative treatment.

[0] Although record linkage of routinely collected health datasets is a valuable research resource, most datasets are established for administrative purposes and not for health outcomes research.
[1] In order for meaningful results to be extrapolated to specific populations, the limitations of the data and linkage methodology need to be investigated and clarified.
[2] It is the objective of this study to investigate the differences in ascertainment which may arise between a hospital admission dataset and a dispensing claims dataset, using major depression in pregnancy as an example.
[3] The safe use of antidepressants in pregnancy is an ongoing issue for clinicians with around 10% of pregnant women suffer from depression.
[4] As the birth admission will be the first admission to hospital during their pregnancy for most women, their use of antidepressants, or their depressive condition, may not be revealed to the attending hospital clinicians.
[5] This may result in adverse outcomes for the mother and infant.
[6] Population-based de-identified data were provided from the Western Australian Data Linkage System linking the administrative health records of women with a delivery to related records from the Midwives' Notification System, the Hospital Morbidity Data System and the national Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme dataset.
[7] The women with depression during their pregnancy were ascertained in two ways: women with dispensing records relating to dispensed antidepressant medicines with an WHO ATC code to the 3rd level, pharmacological subgroup, 'N06A Antidepressants';
[8] and, women with any hospital admission during pregnancy, including the birth admission, if a comorbidity was recorded relating to depression.
[9] From 2002 to 2005, there were 96698 births in WA.
[10] At least one antidepressant was dispensed to 4485 (4.6%) pregnant women.
[11] There were 3010 (3.1%) women with a comorbidity related to depression recorded on their delivery admission, or other admission to hospital during pregnancy.
[12] There were a total of 7495 pregnancies identified by either set of records.
[13] Using data linkage, we determined that these records represented 6596 individual pregnancies.
[14] Only 899 pregnancies were found in both groups (13.6% of all cases).
[15] 80% of women dispensed an antidepressant did not have depression recorded as a comorbidity on their hospital records.
[16] A simple capture-recapture calculation suggests the prevalence of depression in this population of pregnant women to be around 16%.

Optimism and survival: does an optimistic outlook predict better survival at advanced ages?

[0] Studies examining predictors of survival among the oldest-old have primarily focused on objective measures, such as physical function and health status.

[4] At baseline in 1998, a total of 2,262 persons aged 92 or 93 agreed to participate in the intake survey.
[5] The baseline in-person interview consisted of a comprehensive questionnaire including physical functioning and health, and a question about whether the respondent had an optimistic, neutral or pessimistic outlook on his or her own future.
[6] During the follow-up period of 12 years (1998-2010) there were 2,239 deaths (99 %) in the 1905 Cohort Survey.
[7] Univariable analyses revealed that optimistic women and men were at lower risk of death compared to their neutral counterparts [HR 0.82, 95 % CI (0.73-0.93) and 0.81, 95 % CI (0.66-0.99), respectively].
[8] When confounding factors such as baseline physical and cognitive functioning and disease were taken into account the association between optimism and survival weakened in both sexes, but the general pattern persisted.
[9] Optimistic women were still at lower risk of death compared to neutral women [HR 0.85, 95 % CI (0.74-0.97)].
[10] The risk of death was also decreased for optimistic men compared to their neutral counterparts, but the effect was non-significant [HR 0.91, 95 % CI (0.73-1.13)].

[8] Six severe reactions (6 of 174, 3.4%) involving significant hypotension and/or hypoxia that required acute and intensive management occurred during subsequent (i.e.
[9] not the first) transfusion in six patients.

[6] The Pearson correlation test showed correlation between trabecular number, trabecular thickness, BV/TV, trabecular BMD, total BMD, and IT, PTV, and PS.
[7] There was correlation between cortical thickness and IT and PS (P≤.05).

QUESTION:
Is combined therapy more effective than growth hormone or hyperbaric oxygen alone in the healing of left ischemic and non-ischemic colonic anastomoses?

[0] Our aim was to investigate the effects of growth hormone (GH), hyperbaric oxygen and combined therapy on normal and ischemic colonic anastomoses in rats.
[1] Eighty male Wistar rats were divided into eight groups (n = 10).
[2] In the first four groups, non-ischemic colonic anastomosis was performed, whereas in the remaining four groups, ischemic colonic anastomosis was performed.
[3] In groups 5, 6, 7, and 8, colonic ischemia was established by ligating 2 cm of the mesocolon on either side of the anastomosis.
[4] The control groups (1 and 5) received no treatment.
[5] Hyperbaric oxygen therapy was initiated immediately after surgery and continued for 4 days in groups 3 and 4.
[6] Groups 2 and 6 received recombinant human growth hormone, whereas groups 4 and 8 received GH and hyperbaric oxygen treatment.
[7] Relaparotomy was performed on postoperative day 4, and a perianastomotic colon segment 2 cm in length was excised for the detection of biochemical and mechanical parameters of anastomotic healing and histopathological evaluation.
[8] Combined treatment with hyperbaric oxygen and GH increased the mean bursting pressure values in all of the groups, and a statistically significant increase was noted in the ischemic groups compared to the controls (p<0.05).

[4] For the reOSCE stations, student performance was assessed by both a local examiner (LE) in the room and a remote examiner (RE) who viewed the OSCE encounters from a distance.
[5] The primary endpoint was the correlation of scores between LEs and REs across all reOSCE stations.

[9] Correlations on three of the six stations reached significance.
[10] Qualitative analysis of feedback from REs and students showed high acceptance of the reOSCE despite technological issues.

[12] There was a trend to noise increasing with increasing HFNC gas flows.

[8] nighttime surgery, mechanism of injury, and AO and Winquist classifications.

[2] Patients were divided into three groups according to the anterior laxity of the contralateral, normal knee in 30° of knee flexion as measured with a KT2000 arthrometer exerting a force of 134 N:<5 mm for Group 1, 5 to 7.5 mm for Group 2, and>7.5 mm for Group 3.

[5] Functional outcomes were assessed with the Lysholm score and the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) score.
[6] The three groups differed significantly with respect to the postoperative side-to-side difference in anterior laxity (p = 0.015), Lysholm score (p<0.001), and IKDC subjective score (p<0.001).
[7] The mean side-to-side difference in anterior laxity of the reconstructed knee was 2.1 ± 1.3 mm in Group 1, 2.2 ± 1.3 mm in Group 2, and 2.9 ± 1.4 mm in Group 3.
[8] The postoperative Lysholm score was 91.8 ± 4.5 in Group 1, 90.3 ± 5.5 in Group 2, and 85.4 ± 6.6 in Group 3.
[9] The postoperative IKDC subjective score was 89.3 ± 6.4 in Group 1, 87.9 ± 6.0 in Group 2, and 82.6 ± 8.2 in Group 3.
[10] Post hoc testing showed that Group 3 had significantly greater anterior laxity (p ≤ 0.039) and lower functional scores (p ≤ 0.001) compared with Groups 1 and 2.

QUESTION:
MR arthrography of the shoulder: do we need local anesthesia?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] To assess pain intensity with and without subcutaneous local anesthesia prior to intraarticular administration of contrast medium for magnetic resonance arthrography (MRa) of the shoulder.
[1] This single-center study was conducted after an IRB waiver of authorization, between January 2010 and December 2012.
[2] All patients provided written, informed consent for the procedure.
[3] Our prospectively populated institutional database was searched, based on our inclusion criteria.
[4] There were 249 outpatients (178 men and 71 women;
[5] range, 15-79) who underwent MRa and were enrolled in this study.
[6] Patients were excluded if they had received surgery of the shoulder before MRa, had undergone repeated MRa of the same shoulder, and/or had undergone MRa of both shoulders on the same day.
[7] Patients were randomly assigned into one of three groups.
[8] Patients in group A (n=61) received skin infiltration with local anesthesia.
[9] Patients in control group B (n=92) and group C (n=96) did not receive local anesthesia.
[10] Pain levels were immediately assessed after the injection for MRa using a horizontal visual analog scale (VAS) that ranged from 0 to 10.
[11] To compare the pain scores of the three groups for male and female patients, a two-way analysis of variance was used.
[12] A p-value equal to or less than 0.05 was considered to indicate a significant result.
[13] Patients who received local anesthesia (group A) showed a mean pain level on the VAS of 2.6 ± 2.3.
[14] In patients who did not receive local anesthetics (groups B and C), a mean pain level on the VAS of 2.6 ± 2.2 and 2.7 ± 2.4 were detected, respectively.
[15] Between the three groups, no statistically significant difference in pain intensity was detected (p=.960).
[16] There were significant differences in subjective pain perception between men and women (p=.009).
[17] Moreover, the sex difference in all three groups was equal (p=.934).

[2] We reviewed the literature to determine if there is sufficient evidence that dexamethasone can be used as an effective alternative in the treatment of pediatric asthma exacerbations in the inpatient setting.
[3] A Medline search was conducted on the use of dexamethasone in the treatment of asthma exacerbations in children.
[4] The studies selected were clinical trials comparing the efficacy of dexamethasone with prednisone.
[5] Meta-analysis was performed examining physician revisitation rates and symptomatic return to baseline.
[6] Six completed pediatric clinical trials met the inclusion criteria.
[7] All of the pediatric trials found that prednisone is not superior to dexamethasone in treating mild to moderate asthma exacerbations.

[3] This was a cross-sectional study including 560 healthy women aged 19-65 years divided into three age groups.
[4] Correlations were considered to be statistically significant at P<0.05.

[7] Sexual desire correlated overall with FT and androstenedione in the total cohort of women.
[8] In a subgroup of women aged 25-44 years with no use of systemic hormonal contraception, sexual desire correlated with TT, FT, androstenedione, and DHEAS.
[9] In women aged 45-65 years, androstenedione correlated with sexual desire.
[10] No correlations between ADT-G and sexual desire were identified.

[3] Cone-beam computed tomography data were imported into 3-dimensional software.

[8] The bone thicknesses were taken at 45°, 60°, and 90° in relation to the alveolar ridge, simulating a miniscrew insertion.
[9] These factors were evaluated for sexual dimorphism and malocclusion (Angle Classes I and II).
[10] Sexual dimorphism and malocclusion were evaluated with t tests.
[11] To compare the inter-radicular space and the thickness of bone between areas, an analysis of variance for repeated measures was used.
[12] The sample was composed of 100 patients with a mean age of 17.4 ± 6.74 years.
[13] There were 61 female and 39 male patients and 60 Class I and 40 Class II molar relationships.
[14] The inter-radicular space ranged from 2.46 to 3.31 mm, and alveolar bone thickness ranged from 8.01 to 13.77 mm.
[15] The thickness tended to decrease with the increase in insertion angle from 45° to 90°.
[16] No significant differences between the genders or types of malocclusion were found.

Example ID: 25503376
QUESTION:
Does airway surgery lower serum lipid levels in obstructive sleep apnea patients?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is tightly linked to increased cardiovascular disease.
[1] Surgery is an important method to treat OSA, but its effect on serum lipid levels in OSA patients is unknown.
[2] We aimed to evaluate the effect of upper airway surgery on lipid profiles.
[3] We performed a retrospective review of 113 adult patients with OSA who underwent surgery (nasal or uvulopalatopharyngoplasty [UPPP]) at a major, urban, academic hospital in Beijing from 2012 to 2013 who had preoperative and postoperative serum lipid profiles.
[4] Serum TC (4.86±0.74 to 4.69±0.71) and LP(a) (median 18.50 to 10.90) all decreased significantly post-operatively (P<0.01, 0.01, respectively), with no changes in serum HDL, LDL, or TG (P>0.05, all).
[5] For UPPP patients (n=51), serum TC, HDL and LP(a) improved (P=0.01, 0.01,<0.01, respectively).
[6] For nasal patients (n=62), only the serum LP(a) decreased (P<0.01).
[7] In patients with normal serum lipids at baseline, only serum LP(a) decreased (P<0.01).
[8] In contrast, in patients with isolated hypertriglyceridemia, the serum HDL, TG and LP(a) showed significant improvements (P=0.02, 0.03,<0.01, respectively).
[9] In patients with isolated hypercholesterolemia, the serum LP(a) decreased significantly (P=0.01), with a similar trend for serum TC (P=0.06).
[10] In patients with mixed hyperlipidemia, the serum TC and LDL also decreased (P=0.02, 0.03, respectively).

Can transcranial direct current stimulation be useful in differentiating unresponsive wakefulness syndrome from minimally conscious state patients?

[0] Disorders of consciousness (DOC) diagnosis relies on the presence or absence of purposeful motor responsiveness, which characterizes the minimally conscious state (MCS) and the unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS), respectively.
[1] Functional neuroimaging studies have raised the question of possible residual conscious awareness also in clinically-defined UWS patients.
[2] The aim of our study was to identify electrophysiological parameters, by means of a transcranial magnetic stimulation approach, which might potentially express the presence of residual networks sustaining fragmentary behavioral patterns, even when no conscious behavior can be observed.
[3] We enrolled 25 severe DOC patients, following post-anoxic or traumatic brain injury and 20 healthy individuals (HC) as control group.
[4] Baseline electrophysiological evaluation evidenced, in comparison to HC, a partial preservation of cortical effective connectivity and excitability in clinically defined MCS, whereas these components were absent in clinically defined UWS.
[5] Then, we applied an anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (a-tDCS) protocol over the orbitofrontal cortex.
[6] a-tDCS was able to boost cortical connectivity and excitability in all HC, MCS, and to unmask such excitability/connectivity in some UWS patients.

QUESTION:
Is cardiovascular evaluation necessary prior to and during beta-blocker therapy for infantile hemangiomas?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Although consensus guidelines for pretreatment evaluation and monitoring of propranolol therapy in patients with infantile hemangiomas (IH) have been formulated, little is known about the cardiovascular side effects.
[1] We sought to analyze cardiovascular evaluations in patients with IH at baseline and during treatment with an oral beta-blocker.
[2] Data from 109 patients with IH were retrospectively analyzed.
[3] Patient and family history, pretreatment electrocardiogram (ECG), heart rate, and blood pressure were evaluated before initiation of beta-blocker therapy.
[4] Blood pressure and standardized questionnaires addressing side effects were evaluated during treatment.
[5] Questionnaire analyses (n = 83) identified 3 cases with a family history of cardiovascular disease in first-degree relatives.
[6] ECG findings were normal in each case and no serious complication of therapy occurred.
[7] ECG abnormalities were found in 6.5% of patients but there were no contraindications to beta-blocker therapy and no major complications.
[8] Hypotension in 9 patients did not require therapy adjustment.
[9] In all, 88 parents (81%) reported side effects during beta-blocker treatment.
[10] The relatively small patient cohort is a limitation.

[6] At the same time, finger-prick blood was taken for glucometric analysis and subsequent readings were recorded.
[7] The patient's blood glucose values ranged from 74 to 256 mg/dl.
[8] The comparison between gingival crevicular blood and finger-prick blood showed a very strong correlation, with a t value of 3.97 (at P value = 0.001).

[9] Three individual variables, namely 'receiving clinical supervision', 'having some choice in the allocation of clinical supervisor' and 'having a completed clinical supervision agreement', were also significantly associated with higher total MCSS-26 scores (P(s)<0.014).

[2] This study aimed to compare two samples of gay men living with HIV, one recruited via the Web and the other recruited in outpatient settings, in terms of self-reported physical and psychological symptom burden.
[3] The Internet sample was recruited from a UK-wide Web-based survey of gay men with diagnosed HIV.
[4] Of these, 154 respondents identified themselves as resident in London and were included in this analysis.
[5] The HIV clinic sample was recruited from five HIV outpatient clinics.
[6] Of these participants, 400 gay men recruited in London clinics were included in this analysis.
[7] The Web-based sample was younger than the clinic sample (37.3 years, SD 7.0 vs 40.9 years, SD 8.3), more likely to be in paid employment (72.8%, 99/136 vs 60.1%, 227/378), less likely to be on antiretroviral therapy (ART) (58.4%, 90/154 vs 68.0%, 266/391), and had worse mean psychological symptom burden compared to the clinic sample (mean scores: 1.61, SD 1.09 vs 1.36, SD 0.96) but similar physical symptom burden (mean scores: 0.78, SD 0.65 vs 0.70, SD 0.74).
[8] In multivariable logistic regression, for the physical symptom burden model, adjusted for age, ethnicity, employment status, and ART use, the recruitment setting (ie, Web-based vs clinic) was not significantly associated with high physical symptom score.
[9] The only variable that remained significantly associated with high physical symptom score was employment status, with those in employment being less likely to report being in the upper (worst) physical symptom tertile versus the other two tertiles (adjusted OR 0.41, 95% CI 0.28-0.62, P<.001).
[10] For the psychological symptom burden model, those recruited via the Web were significantly more likely to report being in the upper (worst) tertile (adjusted OR 2.20, 95% CI 1.41-3.44, P=.001).
[11] In addition, those in employment were less likely to report being in the upper (worst) psychological symptom tertile compared to those not in employment (adjusted OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.21-0.49, P<.001).

[0] Pregnancy induces adaptations in maternal metabolism to meet the increased need for nutrients by the placenta and fetus.

[3] However, the impact of pregnancy on maternal creatine homeostasis is unclear.

[5] This study aimed to describe maternal creatine homeostasis from mid to late gestation in the precocial spiny mouse.

[10] Plasma creatine and renal creatine excretion decreased significantly from mid to late gestation (P<0.001, P<0.05, respectively).
[11] Pregnancy resulted in increased lean tissue (P<0.01), kidney (P<0.01), liver (P<0.01) and heart (P<0.05) mass at term.
[12] CrT1 expression was increased in the heart (P<0.05) and skeletal muscle (P<0.05) at term compared to non-pregnant tissues, and creatine content of the heart (P<0.05) and kidney (P<0.001) were also increased at this time.
[13] CrT1 mRNA expression was down-regulated in the liver (<0.01) and brain (<0.01) of pregnant spiny mice at term.
[14] Renal AGAT mRNA (P<0.01) and protein (P<0.05) expression were both significantly up-regulated at term, with decreased expression of AGAT mRNA (<0.01) and GAMT protein (<0.05) observed in the term pregnant heart.
[15] Brain AGAT (<0.01) and GAMT (<0.001) mRNA expression were also decreased at term.

[4] Postoperatively all patients were mobilized without weightbearing restrictions.
[5] Indications for immediate THA after acetabular fractures were displaced articular comminution deemed unreducible.
[6] Eleven of the 12 were prospectively studied to evaluate the initial stability of the reconstructions using radiostereometric analysis.
[7] One of the patients died of a pulmonary embolism after surgery, and the remaining 10 (median age, 81 years;
[8] range, 72-86 years) were studied.
[9] Of these, five were analyzed at 1 year and five were analyzed at 2 years.
[10] Acetabular component migration was defined as acceptable if less than the limits for primary THA that predict later loosening (1.76 mm of proximal migration and 2.53° of sagittal rotation).
[11] The contact surface between the acetabular component and ilium in direct continuity with the sacroiliac joint, and the ischium and pubis in direct continuity with the symphysis pubis, was measured on postoperative CT scans.
[12] At 1 year the median proximal migration was 0.83 mm (range, 0.09-5.13 mm) and sagittal rotation was 1.3° (range, 0.1°-7.4°).
[13] Three of the 10 components had migration above the suggested limits for primary THA at 1 year postoperatively.
[14] The contact surface achieved at surgery between the acetabular component and pelvis ranged from 11 to 17 cm(2) (15%-27% of each component).

QUESTION:
Utility of unenhanced fat-suppressed T1-weighted MRI in children with sickle cell disease -- can it differentiate bone infarcts from acute osteomyelitis?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Children with sickle cell disease (SCD) are at risk of bone infarcts and acute osteomyelitis.
[1] The clinical differentiation between a bone infarct and acute osteomyelitis is a diagnostic challenge.
[2] Unenhanced T1-W fat-saturated MR images have been proposed as a potential tool to differentiate bone infarcts from osteomyelitis.
[3] To evaluate the reliability of unenhanced T1-W fat-saturated MRI for differentiation between bone infarcts and acute osteomyelitis in children with SCD.
[4] We retrospectively reviewed the records of 31 children (20 boys, 11 girls;
[5] mean age 10.6 years, range 1.1-17.9 years) with SCD and acute bone pain who underwent MR imaging including unenhanced T1-W fat-saturated images from 2005 to 2010.
[6] Complete clinical charts were reviewed by a pediatric hematologist with training in infectious diseases to determine a clinical standard to define the presence or absence of osteomyelitis.
[7] A pediatric radiologist reviewed all MR imaging and was blinded to clinical information.
[8] Based on the signal intensity in T1-W fat-saturated images, the children were further classified as positive for osteomyelitis (low bone marrow signal intensity) or positive for bone infarct (high bone marrow signal intensity).
[9] Based on the clinical standard, 5 children were classified as positive for osteomyelitis and 26 children as positive for bone infarct (negative for osteomyelitis).
[10] The bone marrow signal intensity on T1-W fat-saturated imaging was not significant for the differentiation between bone infarct and osteomyelitis (P = 0.56).
[11] None of the additional evaluated imaging parameters on unenhanced MRI proved reliable in differentiating these diagnoses.

The Deformity Angular Ratio: Does It Correlate With High-Risk Cases for Potential Spinal Cord Monitoring Alerts in Pediatric 3-Column Thoracic Spinal Deformity Corrective Surgery?

[0] The purpose of this study was to determine whether the deformity angular ratio (DAR) can reliably assess the neurological risks of patients undergoing deformity correction.
[1] Identifying high-risk patients and procedures can help ensure that appropriate measures are taken to minimize neurological complications during spinal deformity corrections.
[2] Subjectively, surgeons look at radiographs and evaluate the riskiness of the procedure.
[3] However, 2 curves of similar magnitude and location can have significantly different risks of neurological deficit during surgery.
[4] Whether the curve spans many levels or just a few can significantly influence surgical strategies.
[5] Lenke et al have proposed the DAR, which is a measure of curve magnitude per level of deformity.
[6] The data from 35 pediatric spinal deformity correction procedures with thoracic 3-column osteotomies were reviewed.
[7] Measurements from preoperative radiographs were used to calculate the DAR.
[8] Binary logistic regression was used to model the relationship between DARs (independent variables) and presence or absence of an intraoperative alert (dependent variable).
[9] In patients undergoing 3-column osteotomies, sagittal curve magnitude and total curve magnitude were associated with increased incidence of transcranial motor evoked potential changes.
[10] Total DAR greater than 45° per level and sagittal DAR greater than 22° per level were associated with a 75% incidence of a motor evoked potential alert, with the incidence increasing to 90% with sagittal DAR of 28° per level.

QUESTION:
Are financial incentives cost-effective to support smoking cessation during pregnancy?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] To investigate the cost-effectiveness of up to £400 worth of financial incentives for smoking cessation in pregnancy as an adjunct to routine health care.
[1] Cost-effectiveness analysis based on a Phase II randomized controlled trial (RCT) and a cost-utility analysis using a life-time Markov model.
[2] The RCT was undertaken in Glasgow, Scotland.
[3] The economic analysis was undertaken from the UK National Health Service (NHS) perspective.
[4] A total of 612 pregnant women randomized to receive usual cessation support plus or minus financial incentives of up to £400 vouchers (US $609), contingent upon smoking cessation.
[5] Comparison of usual support and incentive interventions in terms of cotinine-validated quitters, quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and direct costs to the NHS.
[6] The incremental cost per quitter at 34-38 weeks pregnant was £1127 ($1716).This is similar to the standard look-up value derived from Stapleton&West's published ICER tables, £1390 per quitter, by looking up the Cessation in Pregnancy Incentives Trial (CIPT) incremental cost (£157) and incremental 6-month quit outcome (0.14).
[7] The life-time model resulted in an incremental cost of £17 [95% confidence interval (CI) = -£93, £107] and a gain of 0.04 QALYs (95% CI = -0.058, 0.145), giving an ICER of £482/QALY ($734/QALY).

[14] EBP doctors attended twice as many patients/doctor as SP doctors.

QUESTION:
Cycloplegic autorefraction in young adults: is it mandatory?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] The precise correction of refractive error is especially important in young adults.

[3] This was a prospective study of 1400 eyes (n = 700) of enlisted soldiers aged 18 to 21 years who were consecutively evaluated in an outpatient army ophthalmology clinic.
[4] One drop of cyclopentolate 1 % was installed twice 10 min apart, and cycloplegic refraction was performed in both eyes 40 min later using an auto-refractor.
[5] The difference between non-cycloplegic and cycloplegic refractive measurements was analyzed.
[6] The mean difference in SE between non-cycloplegic and cycloplegic measurements was 0.68 ± 0.83 D (95 % CI, 0.64-0.72).

[8] Moderate hypermetropes (2 to 5 D) demonstrated significantly greater refractive error than mild (0.5 to 2 D) or severe (>5 D) hypermetropes (1.71 ± 1.18 D versus 1.19 ± 0.74 D and 1.16 ± 1.08 D respectively, p < 0.001).

QUESTION:
Is Alveolar Macrophage Phagocytic Dysfunction in Children With Protracted Bacterial Bronchitis a Forerunner to Bronchiectasis?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Children with recurrent protracted bacterial bronchitis (PBB) and bronchiectasis share common features, and PBB is likely a forerunner to bronchiectasis.
[1] Both diseases are associated with neutrophilic inflammation and frequent isolation of potentially pathogenic microorganisms, including nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae (NTHi), from the lower airway.
[2] Defective alveolar macrophage phagocytosis of apoptotic bronchial epithelial cells (efferocytosis), as found in other chronic lung diseases, may also contribute to tissue damage and neutrophil persistence.
[3] Thus, in children with bronchiectasis or PBB and in control subjects, we quantified the phagocytosis of airway apoptotic cells and NTHi by alveolar macrophages and related the phagocytic capacity to clinical and airway inflammation.
[4] Children with bronchiectasis (n = 55) or PBB (n = 13) and control subjects (n = 13) were recruited.
[5] Alveolar macrophage phagocytosis, efferocytosis, and expression of phagocytic scavenger receptors were assessed by flow cytometry.
[6] Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid interleukin (IL) 1β was measured by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
[7] For children with PBB or bronchiectasis, macrophage phagocytic capacity was significantly lower than for control subjects (P = .003 and P<.001 for efferocytosis and P = .041 and P = .004 for phagocytosis of NTHi;
[8] PBB and bronchiectasis, respectively);
[9] median phagocytosis of NTHi for the groups was as follows: bronchiectasis, 13.7% (interquartile range [IQR], 11%-16%);
[10] control subjects, 19.0% (IQR, 13%-21%);
[11] and median efferocytosis for the groups was as follows: bronchiectasis, 14.1% (IQR, 10%-16%);
[12] control subjects, 18.1% (IQR, 16%-21%).
[13] Mannose receptor expression was significantly reduced in the bronchiectasis group (P = .019), and IL-1β increased in both bronchiectasis and PBB groups vs control subjects.

Example ID: 26923375
QUESTION:
Is non-invasive diagnosis of esophageal varices in patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis possible by duplex Doppler ultrasonography?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Esophageal varices are present in 30% to 40% of patients in compensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class A) and in 60% to 85% of patients in decompensated cirrhosis (Child-Pugh classes B and C).
[1] It is important to identify patients with compensated cirrhosis at risk for esophageal varix development.
[2] We evaluated the accuracy of a duplex Doppler ultrasonographic index for predicting the presence or absence of esophageal varices in patients with compensated hepatic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh class A) by using endoscopy as the reference standard.
[3] Fifty-six enrolled patients underwent duplex Doppler ultrasonography followed by screening endoscopy.
[4] Mean portal vein velocity (PVV), splenic index (SI), splenoportal index (SPI), hepatic and splenic arterial resistive, and pulsatility indices (hepatic artery resistive index [HARI], hepatic artery pulsatility index [HAPI], splenic artery resistive index [SARI], splenic artery pulsatility index [SAPI]) were recorded.
[5] Univariate logistic regression analysis was followed by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve construction for the indices that were significant.
[6] The indices HARI, HAPI, SARI, SAPI were not helpful (p > 0.05).
[7] Mean PVV, SI, and SPI were all predictive of the presence of esophageal varices (p < 0.05) and SPI was found to be the most accurate parameter.
[8] Of the various cut-off levels of SPI evaluated, a cut-off value of SPI at 5.0, offered the highest diagnostic accuracy (88%).
