QUESTION:
Could chest wall rigidity be a factor in rapid death from illicit fentanyl abuse?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] There has been a significant spike in fentanyl-related deaths from illicit fentanyl supplied via the heroin trade.
[1] Past fentanyl access was primarily oral or dermal via prescription fentanyl patch diversion.
[2] One factor potentially driving this increase in fatalities is the change in route of administration.
[3] Rapid intravenous (IV) fentanyl can produce chest wall rigidity.
[4] We evaluated post-mortem fentanyl and norfentanyl concentrations in a recent surge of lethal fentanyl intoxications.
[5] Fentanyl related deaths from the Franklin County coroner's office from January to September 2015 were identified.
[6] Presumptive positive fentanyl results were confirmed by quantitative analysis using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS/MS) and were able to quantify fentanyl, norfentanyl, alfentanyl, and sufentanyl.
[7] 48 fentanyl deaths were identified.
[8] Mean fentanyl concentrations were 12.5 ng/ml, (range 0.5 ng/ml to >40 ng/ml).
[9] Mean norfentanyl concentrations were 1.9 ng/ml (range none detected to 8.3 ng/ml).
[10] No appreciable concentrations of norfentanyl could be detected in 20 of 48 cases (42%) and were less than 1 ng/ml in 25 cases (52%).
[11] Elevated fentanyl concentrations did not correlate with rises in norfentanyl levels.
[12] In several cases fentanyl concentrations were strikingly high (22 ng/ml and 20 ng/ml) with no norfentanyl detected.
[13] The lack of any measurable norfentanyl in half of our cases suggests a very rapid death, consistent with acute chest rigidity.
[14] An alternate explanation could be a dose-related rapid onset of respiratory arrest.
[15] Deaths occurred with low levels of fentanyl in the therapeutic range (1-2 ng/ml) in apparent non-naïve opiate abusers.
[16] Acute chest wall rigidity is a well-recognized complication in the medical community but unknown within the drug abuse community.
[17] The average abuser of illicit opioids may be unaware of the increasing fentanyl content of their illicit opioid purchase.

Example ID: 27078715
QUESTION:
Digital Tomosynthesis: A Viable Alternative to Noncontrast Computed Tomography for the Follow-Up of Nephrolithiasis?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Digital tomosynthesis (DT) is a new X-ray-based imaging technique that allows image enhancement with minimal increase in radiation exposure.
[1] The purpose of this study was to compare DT with noncontrast computed tomography (NCCT) and to evaluate its potential role for the follow-up of patients with nephrolithiasis in a nonemergent setting.
[2] A retrospective review of patients with nephrolithiasis at our institution that underwent NCCT and DT from July 2012 to September 2013 was performed.
[3] Renal units (RUs) that did not undergo treatment or stone passage were randomly assigned to two blinded readers, who recorded stone count, size area (mm(2)), maximum stone length (mm), and location, for both DT and NCCT.
[4] Mean differences per RU were compared.
[5] Potential variables affecting stone detection rate, including stone size and body mass index (BMI), were evaluated.
[6] Interobserver agreement was determined using the intraclass correlation coefficient to measure the consistency of measurements made by the readers.
[7] DT and NCCT demonstrated similar stone detection rates in terms of stone counts and stone area mm(2).
[8] Of the 79 RUs assessed, 41 RUs showed exact stone counts on DT and NCCT.
[9] The mean difference in stone area was 16.5 mm(2) (-4.6 to 38.5), p = 0.121.
[10] The mean size of the largest stone on NCCT and DT was 9.27 and 8.87 mm, respectively.
[11] Stone size and BMI did not cause a significant difference in stone detection rates.
[12] Interobserver agreement showed a strong correlation between readers and adequate reproducibility.

QUESTION:
Do risk calculators accurately predict surgical site occurrences?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Current risk assessment models for surgical site occurrence (SSO) and surgical site infection (SSI) after open ventral hernia repair (VHR) have limited external validation.
[1] Our aim was to determine (1) whether existing models stratify patients into groups by risk and (2) which model best predicts the rate of SSO and SSI.
[2] Patients who underwent open VHR and were followed for at least 1 mo were included.
[3] Using two data sets-a retrospective multicenter database (Ventral Hernia Outcomes Collaborative) and a single-center prospective database (Prospective)-each patient was assigned a predicted risk with each of the following models: Ventral Hernia Risk Score (VHRS), Ventral Hernia Working Group (VHWG), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Wound Class, and Hernia Wound Risk Assessment Tool (HW-RAT).
[4] Patients in the Prospective database were also assigned a predicted risk from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program (ACS-NSQIP).
[5] Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (area under the curve [AUC]) were compared to assess the predictive accuracy of the models for SSO and SSI.
[6] Pearson's chi-square was used to determine which models were able to risk-stratify patients into groups with significantly differing rates of actual SSO and SSI.
[7] The Ventral Hernia Outcomes Collaborative database (n = 795) had an overall SSO and SSI rate of 23% and 17%, respectively.
[8] The AUCs were low for SSO (0.56, 0.54, 0.52, and 0.60) and SSI (0.55, 0.53, 0.50, and 0.58).
[9] The VHRS (P = 0.01) and HW-RAT (P < 0.01) significantly stratified patients into tiers for SSO, whereas the VHWG (P < 0.05) and HW-RAT (P < 0.05) stratified for SSI.
[10] In the Prospective database (n = 88), 14% and 8% developed an SSO and SSI, respectively.
[11] The AUCs were low for SSO (0.63, 0.54, 0.50, 0.57, and 0.69) and modest for SSI (0.81, 0.64, 0.55, 0.62, and 0.73).

[0] In the prehospital setting, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) professionals rely on providing positive pressure ventilation with a bag-valve-mask (BVM).

[2] Our primary objective was to determine if a group of EMS professionals could provide ventilations with a smaller BVM that would be sufficient to ventilate patients.
[3] Secondary objectives included 1) if the pediatric bag provided volumes similar to lung-protective ventilation in the hospital setting and 2) compare volumes provided to the patient depending on the type of airway (mask, King tube, and intubation).
[4] Using a patient simulator of a head and thorax that was able to record respiratory rate, tidal volume, peak pressure, and minute volume via a laptop computer, participants were asked to ventilate the simulator during six 1-minute ventilation tests.
[5] The first scenario was BVM ventilation with an oropharyngeal airway in place ventilating with both an adult- and pediatric-sized BVM, the second scenario had a supraglottic airway and both bags, and the third scenario had an endotracheal tube and both bags.
[6] Participants were enrolled in convenience manner while they were on-duty and the research staff was able to travel to their stations.
[7] Prior to enrolling, participants were not given any additional training on ventilation skills.
[8] We enrolled 50 providers from a large, busy, urban fire-based EMS agency with 14.96 (SD = 9.92) mean years of experience.
[9] Only 1.5% of all breaths delivered with the pediatric BVM during the ventilation scenarios were below the recommended tidal volume.
[10] A greater percentage of breaths delivered in the recommended range occurred when the pediatric BVM was used (17.5% vs 5.1%, p<0.001).

[11] The intraclass correlation coefficient between the radiologists involved was 0.78.
[12] Muscle oedema was more common in DM than in PM except in the posterior thigh muscles.
[13] In particular, 68% of patients with DM had involvement of at least one anterior thigh muscle versus 38% of patients with PM (p=0.02).
